passage:
9 November.
Mohit was late today. Twenty minutes. Old me would have spiralled: he's bored of me, he's found someone better, typical. I felt it start, that cold drop. Then I remembered the last eight months. Every Sunday he has turned up. When he can't, he texts. Once he rode across Pune in the rain because I panicked about my scholarship. So I wrote on my hand: "Evidence says traffic." And it was traffic. He came in grumbling about a lorry. Dr Kulkarni says I'm rewriting the rulebook my childhood gave me, where promises broke all the time. It's slow. But tonight I just said "Chai?" instead of crying.
Aadhya

qa.q: How late was Mohit?
qa.a: He was twenty minutes late.

qa.q: What did Aadhya feel when Mohit was late, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Aadhya felt a cold drop of fear and began thinking Mohit was bored or had found someone better.

qa.q: What turning point helped Aadhya stay calm?
qa.a: Aadhya remembered eight months of Mohit turning up and wrote "Evidence says traffic", using his past reliability to check the old fear.

qa.q: How might Mohit experience Aadhya's simple "Chai?" compared with the old spiral?
qa.a: He probably feels relaxed and trusted rather than accused, which makes being late less stressful for him.

grounding: A young adult with an unreliable childhood uses a partner's steady track record and therapy to calm an old fear of abandonment.

passage: In her first year at the agricultural college in Dharwad, Swati apologised for everything and expected to be dropped by everyone. Growing up, her father's moods had decided whether home felt safe. Vaibhav-sir, her soil-science mentor, was dull in the best way: office hours every Tuesday, replies within a day, the same calm voice whether her samples were perfect or ruined. When she lost a whole batch to mould, she waited for the explosion. He said, "Happens. Let's see why." By third year she noticed something: when her roommate went quiet, Swati no longer assumed it was about her. She wrote in her notebook, "People can be steady. I can be too."

qa.q: What happened to Swati's batch of samples?
qa.a: She lost a whole batch to mould.

qa.q: What was Swati expecting when she lost the batch, and why?
qa.a: She was afraid of an explosion, because her father's moods had made home feel unsafe.

qa.q: What helped Swati become more secure?
qa.a: Vaibhav-sir's steady reliability over time, plus her own reflection on how her past shaped her expectations.

qa.q: How might Swati's roommate experience the change in her?
qa.a: The roommate probably finds Swati calmer and easier to be around, since quiet moments no longer feel like a threat to her.

grounding: Shows a young adult with an insecure past becoming more secure through a steady mentor and reflecting on old patterns.

passage: Zanele had moved between three aunties' houses before she was twelve, and in her first year at university in Cape Town she kept friendships at arm's length, ready to leave first. Selin, her lab partner, didn't seem to notice the walls. She saved Zanele a seat every Monday, texted when she said she would, and remembered her exams. When Zanele snapped at her over a lost file, Selin said, "That stung. Coffee later?" and meant it. Zanele also started seeing a counsellor on campus, drawing a map of all those houses. By second year she caught herself texting Selin first, without rehearsing. "I think I'm learning people come back," she told the counsellor, surprised.

qa.q: How many aunties' houses had Zanele moved between?
qa.a: Three.

qa.q: How did Zanele feel when she caught herself texting Selin first?
qa.a: She felt surprised and more trusting, starting to believe people come back.

qa.q: Which two things helped Zanele change?
qa.a: Selin's steady reliability and the counsellor helping her reflect on her past moves.

qa.q: What is it like for Selin when Zanele snaps at her?
qa.a: Selin feels stung but stays warm, naming the hurt and still offering coffee.

grounding: Illustrates earned security through a reliable friend and a counsellor who helps a young adult reflect on past patterns.

passage: In the counselling centre's small blue room, Anjali watched the clock the way she always had, waiting for Leela to get bored of her. It was their twentieth session. Leela had never once been late, never cancelled without a week's warning, and hadn't flinched when Anjali shouted in session six. Today Anjali said, "My mother used to disappear for days. I think I test everyone to see if they'll do the same." Leela nodded. "And what have you noticed here?" Anjali was quiet. "You keep coming back. It's boring, actually." They both laughed. Walking out past the reception desk, Anjali noticed she hadn't looked at the clock once.

qa.q: Which session was it?
qa.a: Their twentieth session.

qa.q: What was Anjali afraid of when she watched the clock?
qa.a: She feared Leela would get bored and leave, the way her mother used to disappear.

qa.q: What made Leela's help work over time?
qa.a: Her steady reliability and questions that helped Anjali reflect on her pattern of testing people.

qa.q: How might Leela see Anjali's joke about it being boring?
qa.a: Leela likely sees it as a sign of growing trust, since Anjali is noticing that reliability is real.

grounding: Shows a young adult gaining security through a therapist's reliability and reflection on childhood patterns.

passage:
Dear Amandeep,
It's three years since we met in the hostel queue, and I wanted to write this down properly.
You know what home was like: some days warm, some days nobody spoke to me. So I grew up waiting for people to disappear. In first year, when you didn't reply for a day, I assumed you were done with me and stopped talking to you first.
But you kept turning up. Every Thursday, chai at the canteen, even when I was rude. When I cancelled, you just said, "Next Thursday, then." Slowly I stopped bracing.
My counsellor asked me last month what changed. I said, "Amandeep never disappeared." Now when someone goes quiet, I notice the old fear, and I ask instead of running.
Thank you for being boringly reliable. I mean that as the biggest compliment.
Tanvir

qa.q: What did Tanvir and Amandeep do every Thursday?
qa.a: They had chai at the canteen.

qa.q: How did Tanvir feel in first year when Amandeep didn't reply for a day?
qa.a: Tanvir felt insecure and afraid of being left, assuming Amandeep was done and pulling away first.

qa.q: What helped Tanvir become more secure?
qa.a: Amandeep's repeated reliability, plus talking with a counsellor and noticing the old fear, helped Tanvir ask instead of running.

qa.q: How might Amandeep feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Amandeep would likely feel touched and glad to learn that simply showing up every Thursday, even when Tanvir was rude, mattered so much.

grounding: Shows a young adult from an unpredictable home becoming more secure through a friend's steady reliability and reflection with a counsellor.
